paragraphs: A comorbidity index compresses information about a patient’s diagnoses into a score used for comparing risk and grouping patients. Traditional scores emphasize mortality and use fixed, linear rules. This paper asks whether one learned number can capture more flexible relationships with several clinical outcomes, making the summary useful beyond the outcome around which older indices were designed.

The proposed Machine-Learned Comorbidity Index maps diagnosis codes to a single numerical value. Training maximizes normalized Hilbert–Schmidt Independence Criterion, a measure of statistical dependence, between that score and multiple outcomes. This objective allows the score to reflect nonlinear relationships. The accompanying theory characterizes when an informative ordering of hospital admissions can be shared across outcomes; it does not assert that every collection of outcomes admits such an ordering.

Across multiple benchmark electronic health record datasets, the learned index outperforms strong baselines on multiple evaluation metrics. The stated result supports learning a compact risk summary directly from outcome relationships while retaining the practical simplicity of a single score.
icml-2026-a-machine-learned-comorbidity-.tldr: MLCI learns a single diagnosis-based score that captures nonlinear relationships with multiple clinical outcomes and improves benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Furthest-neighbor search asks which stored point lies farthest from a query, with approximate search allowing a controlled departure from the exact answer. This paper studies a demanding setting: each new query can depend on answers to earlier queries. Such feedback can undermine randomized search methods whose guarantees assume queries are chosen without observing the system’s previous responses.

The authors construct an adversarially robust data structure for c-approximate furthest-neighbor queries. For n points in d dimensions, its query time is approximately the smaller of d times n raised to 1/c² and n raised to 2/c² plus d, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Its dependence on n matches the cited classical result for queries without adaptive feedback.

The new bound also improves on the cited adaptive distance-estimation approach across a wide range of natural parameter choices. Complementing the construction, the authors give an adaptive attack against the classical furthest-neighbor data structure. Together, these results show both why adaptivity requires attention and how efficient approximate search can accommodate it.
icml-2026-adversarially-robust-approxima.tldr: A new approximate furthest-neighbor data structure preserves guarantees under adaptive queries while matching classical dependence on dataset size.

paragraphs: When people repeatedly use an AI system or shop in a marketplace, trying unfamiliar options can benefit their later decisions. This paper models that situation as a shared multi-armed bandit process in which each self-interested agent controls a short episode of consecutive choices. Because an agent makes several decisions, it can have a personal incentive to explore during its episode.

The central result is that this individual incentive does not ensure effective exploration for the population over time. Under the studied dynamics, aggregate learning can fail, with Bayesian regret growing linearly. That means the cumulative cost of imperfect decisions keeps growing at a constant-order rate. The authors establish that this failure is typical in their setting, rather than confined to a specially constructed worst case.

The conclusion also persists when episode utility is a fixed function such as the minimum or maximum round outcome, rather than a sum. Within this model, organic exploration therefore does not remove the need for externally driven exploration.
icml-2026-bandit-social-learning-with-ex.tldr: In the studied social-learning model, personally useful exploration within short episodes still fails to produce effective collective learning.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets multiple clients train a model while keeping their raw data separate. Those contributors may later need evidence that a suspect model came from their joint work. Embedding a separate watermark for every client can weaken detection as participation grows, while giving one client the entire verification key concentrates control over the shared watermark.

This paper introduces threshold watermarking: all K clients help embed one watermark, but at least t clients must cooperate to reconstruct its key. Secret sharing prevents smaller coalitions from reconstructing the key, and verification can take place without exposing it in clear form. The design makes verification a collective capability whose required coalition size is set by the threshold.

The authors implement the protocol with access to model weights and evaluate image classification under both similar and heterogeneous client data partitions, plus language-model fine-tuning. Detection remains effective with 128 clients and minimal accuracy loss. In tested attacks, including adaptive fine-tuning with up to 20% of training data, the watermark stays above the stated detection threshold.
icml-2026-collaborative-threshold-waterm.tldr: A shared federated-learning watermark requires a threshold coalition to verify provenance and remains detectable in the reported scaling and attack tests.

paragraphs: Combining several AI judges is useful only if their agreement is interpreted appropriately. Judges may share training data, architectures, prompts, and failure modes, so their votes can carry overlapping information. This paper studies binary label aggregation when the usual assumption of independent judgments, conditional on the true answer, does not hold.

The authors use Ising graphical models and latent factors to represent dependencies between judges. When interactions differ by the true class, optimal decision log-odds generally include pairwise products of votes. When the interactions are class-independent, the rule simplifies to a weighted vote, but its weights must account for correlation. Thus, dependence can change either the aggregation rule’s form or the parameters needed to use it correctly.

Constructed examples show that independence-based methods can choose the wrong Bayes label even when individual judges’ marginal behavior is matched. Under latent-factor models, the authors also prove that excess risk can persist as more judges are added. Evaluations on three real-world datasets report improvements over classical aggregation baselines.
icml-2026-dependence-aware-label-aggrega.tldr: Modeling dependencies among AI judges improves label aggregation and explains why adding correlated judges need not eliminate prediction errors.

paragraphs: Sampling from a distribution with several separated regions of high probability becomes especially challenging when adding coordinates refines an underlying function-space model. An algorithm should ideally remain controlled as that approximation grows. This paper investigates when continuous-time annealed Langevin dynamics can achieve such stability for targets that are mixtures of Gaussians.

The analysis follows an explicit path that gradually removes Gaussian smoothing from the target distribution. The authors identify spectral conditions connecting the smoothing covariance with the covariances of the mixture components. Under those conditions, the process reaches a prescribed Kullback–Leibler divergence accuracy within a time horizon that is uniform across dimensions. The result gives conditions for dimension-independent control rather than an unconditional guarantee for multimodal targets.

The paper also analyzes a perturbative setting with imperfect initialization and approximate scores. For a particular misspecified-mixture score model, a preconditioning operator with sufficiently fast spectral decay prevents coordinatewise errors from accumulating. This explains how appropriately chosen preconditioning can preserve the dimension-uniform guarantee despite those approximation errors.
icml-2026-dimension-free-multimodal-samp.tldr: The paper establishes conditions under which continuous-time annealed Langevin sampling of Gaussian mixtures maintains accuracy uniformly across dimensions.

paragraphs: A safety filter divides generated outputs into those it accepts and those it rejects. Fine-tuning a generator simply to avoid rejection can leave its outputs clustered close to that dividing line. The paper argues that this behavior can make filtering less reliable, increasing both the rejection of acceptable outputs and the acceptance of undesirable ones.

Boundary Guidance changes the reinforcement-learning objective so that generation is explicitly steered away from the classifier’s margin. The important distinction is between obtaining an accepted classification and avoiding the uncertain region around the classification boundary. By making that separation part of training, the method addresses a weakness of optimizing only the probability that an output passes the filter.

The authors evaluate the method on jailbreak, ambiguous, and long-context prompts. LLM-as-a-Judge assessments report better safety while utility is maintained or improved. Ablations spanning model scales and reward designs support the approach’s robustness in the tested settings. These findings concern the reported classifier-guided training and evaluations, rather than establishing that filtering errors disappear.
icml-2026-dont-walk-the-line-boundary-gu.tldr: Boundary Guidance trains generators to avoid safety-classifier margins, improving judged safety while preserving or improving utility in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Sparse mixture-of-experts models can keep many parameters while activating only a subset for each input. Converting an existing dense language model offers an alternative to training such a system from scratch. The difficult step is deciding how to divide its feed-forward neurons into experts and how to route tokens among those experts.

DOT-MoE treats neuron assignment as a balanced optimal-transport problem that can be learned during training. Differentiable Sinkhorn–Knopp iterations enforce expert capacity constraints, so the partition respects prescribed sizes. Straight-through estimators allow the discrete assignments and token-routing policy to be optimized together. This connects the construction of experts to the decisions that determine how they will actually be used.

Across multiple architectures and benchmarks, the method outperforms the reported structured-pruning, heuristic-clustering, and random-splitting baselines. The authors report retaining 90% of the original dense model’s performance while reducing active parameters by 50%. This describes a measured performance–computation tradeoff: the reduction concerns parameters used during computation, and the retained performance is below the full dense-model level.
icml-2026-dot-moe-differentiable-optimal.tldr: DOT-MoE jointly learns balanced expert partitions and token routing, retaining 90% of dense-model performance with 50% fewer active parameters.

paragraphs: Continuous-depth neural networks describe transformations using differential equations, but repeatedly solving many nonlinear equations can make training and inference expensive. This paper introduces Continuous Depth Acceleration, or CoDA, to replace those costly layer computations with a more compact combination of recurrent, linear-dynamics, and dense components.

Drawing on Mori–Zwanzig and Koopman operator theory, CoDA substitutes a small GRU module, one low-dimensional linear ordinary differential equation, and a dense layer for a continuous-depth layer requiring multiple nonlinear equations. The authors prove a PAC learnability result supporting accuracy preservation. They also establish that the transformation can be repeated across multiple layers while retaining a unified backpropagation procedure.

On the Liquid Foundation Model LFM-1.2B, the reported experiments show 6.7-fold faster training and 1.8-fold faster inference without accuracy loss. Across six real-world liquid-time-constant network applications, CoDA also beats the tested acceleration techniques in training and inference time while maintaining competitive or better accuracy. The contribution combines a theoretically supported replacement with measured computational savings in those evaluated models and applications.
icml-2026-efficient-continuous-depth-mod.tldr: CoDA replaces expensive continuous-depth computations with compact GRU-based modules and linear dynamics, producing substantial measured speedups while preserving accuracy.

paragraphs: Sensitive text collections can be valuable for developing models even when the original records cannot be shared. Private synthetic-data generation aims to provide useful substitutes, but existing approaches can demand large private datasets and substantial computation. EPSVec addresses this by concentrating the privacy-sensitive work into a single extraction and sanitization stage.

The method builds dataset vectors: directions in a language model’s activation space that summarize how the private data distribution differs from public priors. Once sanitized with differential privacy, these vectors steer ordinary decoding. Generation therefore does not consume additional privacy budget for each new synthetic sample. The authors also use pretrained base models and fixed-shot prompting to improve the diversity and fidelity of generated text.

Experiments report better distributional alignment and downstream utility than existing baselines, particularly when little private data is available, alongside substantially lower computational overhead. The key practical result is that a reusable private steering representation can support repeated generation. The no-additional-privacy-cost claim applies to generation from the vectors after the initial private extraction and sanitization.
icml-2026-epsvec-efficient-and-private-s.tldr: EPSVec privately extracts reusable activation-space steering vectors, enabling efficient synthetic text generation without additional privacy cost per sample.

paragraphs: Best-arm identification means gathering observations to determine which available option is best. In the fixed-confidence version, an algorithm targets a specified reliability level and collects the observations it needs. In the fixed-budget version, the observation budget is set in advance. This paper asks how the difficulty of these formulations compares for general, potentially structured problems.

The authors introduce FC2FB, a meta-algorithm that converts a fixed-confidence algorithm into a fixed-budget algorithm. Its sample-complexity guarantee matches that of the supplied algorithm up to logarithmic factors. The result is constructive: an existing method for one formulation becomes an ingredient for solving the other, rather than merely serving as evidence for an abstract comparison.

Consequently, optimal fixed-confidence sample complexity upper-bounds optimal fixed-budget sample complexity up to those factors. This establishes a one-way relationship, not an exact equality between the settings. Combining the conversion with existing state-of-the-art fixed-confidence algorithms also yields improved sample complexity for several fixed-budget problems, making progress in the former setting useful in the latter.
icml-2026-fixed-budget-is-no-harder-than.tldr: FC2FB converts fixed-confidence best-arm identification algorithms into fixed-budget algorithms with matching sample complexity up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to maintain a valuable selection of at most k items while the available items change. The objective is submodular, meaning that adding an item has diminishing marginal benefit as the selected set grows. It is also non-monotone, so adding an item can decrease value. A fully dynamic algorithm must handle both additions and removals.

The first proposed algorithm guarantees a 0.262 approximation, meaning its maintained solution achieves the stated fraction of the optimum under the guarantee. Its worst-case expected update time is O(ε⁻³k log(k) log(ε⁻¹k) + ε⁻²k² log(k)), with an error parameter ε between zero and one. This improves the approximation factor over the two prior results described in the abstract, which provided factors of approximately 0.125 and 0.171.

A second algorithm raises the approximation guarantee to 0.277 while retaining update time polynomial in k and the inverse error parameter. The contribution offers stronger provable solution quality for changing datasets, with explicit computational bounds rather than relying on repeatedly solving the problem from scratch.
icml-2026-improved-dynamic-algorithm-for.tldr: Two dynamic algorithms improve approximation guarantees for cardinality-constrained non-monotone submodular maximization to 0.262 and 0.277.

paragraphs: Tabular foundation models make predictions for structured tables using information supplied in context, but how those predictions develop inside their transformer layers remains poorly understood. This paper investigates inference across depth in six state-of-the-art models. The goal is to connect their internal computations to the architectural capacity they actually appear to use.

The study tracks how predictions emerge, identifies distinct stages of inference, and examines changes in latent representations. It finds dynamics that differ from those observed in language models. Across multiple tabular models, substantial computations overlap across depth, suggesting that successive layers partly perform iterative refinement rather than wholly distinct operations. This is evidence of redundancy in the studied systems, not a claim that depth never contributes.

Motivated by these observations, the authors build a proof-of-concept model that repeatedly applies a single layer. It uses only 20% of the original model’s parameters while achieving comparable performance. The result links mechanistic analysis to a concrete parameter-saving design and shows why repeated computation can be worth exploring for tabular inference.
icml-2026-is-one-layer-enough-understand.tldr: Layerwise analysis reveals redundant computation in tabular foundation models and motivates a looped single-layer prototype with 20% of the original parameters.

paragraphs: In a Stackelberg game, a leader chooses a strategy while anticipating a follower’s response. Learning becomes harder when the follower’s type is unknown. This paper studies structured versions of these games in which contextual information can help predict that type, allowing the leader to use context when learning a policy that maximizes utility.

For online learning, the authors show that standard measures of learning complexity do not characterize the leader’s difficulty. They introduce the Stackelberg–Littlestone dimension, inspired by a complexity measure from online classification. This new quantity tightly characterizes instance-optimal regret, connecting the structure of a particular learning problem to the performance that an algorithm can achieve. They use it to construct a provably optimal online algorithm.

The paper also studies a distributional setting and introduces two additional dimensions that control sample-complexity upper and lower bounds. Together, the results give tailored ways to measure learning difficulty in these strategic interactions. The role of context is made mathematically explicit rather than treated merely as an extra input feature.
icml-2026-learning-in-structured-stackel.tldr: New complexity measures characterize how leaders can learn effective policies when context predicts an unknown follower type in structured Stackelberg games.

paragraphs: Many difficult discrete optimization problems can be expressed as generalized Ising problems, including MAX-CUT, number partitioning, and maximum independent set. This paper focuses on one-flip local minima: configurations whose objective cannot be improved by changing just one variable. The challenge is to connect these discrete solutions to a smooth objective that gradient-based methods can search.

The authors construct a polynomial relaxation and prove a landscape-equivalence theorem. Every local minimum of the relaxed function corresponds to a one-flip local minimum of the original Ising problem, and the correspondence works in both directions. This gives the continuous landscape a precise relationship to the discrete one, rather than merely hoping that solutions transfer usefully after relaxation.

The smooth formulation permits scalable optimizers such as ADAM, and experiments report strong performance on spin-glass, MAX-CUT, and number-partitioning benchmarks. The guarantee concerns local minima, so it does not make every recovered solution globally optimal. Its significance is preserving a meaningful discrete notion of local optimality while opening the problem to gradient-based optimization.
icml-2026-local-minima-preserving-polyno.tldr: A polynomial relaxation exactly matches its local minima to one-flip Ising minima, enabling gradient-based search with a precise discrete interpretation.

paragraphs: A language model’s mathematical argument becomes more trustworthy when a formal verifier can check it. Interactive theorem provers often require detailed proof steps, whereas auto-active verifiers automate more low-level reasoning but have primarily been used for software. This paper brings mathematical theorem proving into the latter setting by translating the miniF2F benchmark into Dafny.

The resulting miniF2F-Dafny benchmark separates what the verifier can establish automatically from what language-model guidance contributes. Dafny alone solves 39–44% of problems with empty proofs. This indicates that its automation can handle a substantial portion of the benchmark without generated proof guidance, even though many such problems require substantial guidance in interactive theorem provers.

The authors evaluate eight off-the-shelf language models. Claude Opus 4.6 achieves the best reported full-test result, 62.7% cumulative pass@4, compared with a 38.9% empty-proof baseline—a 23.8-percentage-point improvement. The findings support a complementary division of work: models supply higher-level guidance while SMT automation resolves low-level details, with the benchmark and evaluation infrastructure made publicly available.
icml-2026-minif2f-dafny-llm-guided-mathe.tldr: miniF2F-Dafny shows that automated verification can solve many benchmark theorems unaided, with LLM guidance improving the best reported result to 62.7% pass@4.

paragraphs: A generated action trajectory can look useful for a task yet conflict with how the controlled system actually moves. This mismatch limits diffusion-based planning from offline data. Model Predictive Diffuser, or MPDiffuser, addresses it by combining a diffusion planner with a separate diffusion model of system dynamics during trajectory generation.

Sampling alternates between planner updates and dynamics updates. The planner contributes task intent, while the dynamics model progressively corrects feasibility. A lightweight ranking module then selects trajectories that best meet task objectives. The architecture also lets the dynamics component learn from diverse and previously unseen data independently of the planner, which the authors identify as a source of improved sample efficiency and adaptability.

Experiments report consistent improvements over earlier diffusion-based methods on both unconstrained D4RL tasks and constrained DSRL tasks. Deployment on a real quadrupedal robot provides an additional practical demonstration. The central contribution is to incorporate dynamics correction throughout sampling, producing trajectories that better combine task alignment with dynamic plausibility in the evaluated settings.
icml-2026-model-based-diffusion-sampling.tldr: MPDiffuser interleaves task planning with learned dynamics corrections to improve diffusion-generated control trajectories on benchmarks and a quadrupedal robot.

paragraphs: Single-cell RNA sequencing measures gene expression in individual cells, but temporal datasets provide snapshots rather than genuine trajectories of the same cells. Reconstructing a changing population therefore requires inferring movement between distributions. This paper proposes a generative framework designed to represent both population trends and the biological variability hidden within those snapshots.

A latent heteroscedastic Gaussian process models temporal trends while allowing variability to change, with Hilbert-space methods providing an approximation. An optimal-transport objective aligns generated populations with observed ones, avoiding a requirement for known cell-to-cell trajectories. Cell-specific latent time represents asynchronous progression, while cell-type conditioning helps distinguish trajectories toward different cell types. These components separate variation in timing from variation in developmental direction.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance on challenging interpolation and extrapolation benchmarks, covering predictions within and beyond observed time points. They also introduce a gradient-based method for inferring perturbation trajectories. The contribution is a population-level temporal model that explicitly represents heterogeneity while learning from observations that do not directly reveal individual cell histories.
icml-2026-modeling-temporal-scrna-seq-da.tldr: A latent Gaussian-process model with optimal transport reconstructs temporal cell-population changes while explicitly accounting for asynchronous progression and cell types.

paragraphs: An interpretable circuit found in one language model may not reappear in another model trained with the same architecture. This paper investigates that uncertainty by comparing attention-head representations across independently initialized training runs. The study examines models of varying size and complexity, asking how reproducible their internal components are at different depths.

The experiments find that middle-layer heads are least stable across runs while also being most distinct in their representations. Greater model depth brings stronger divergence around the middle. In deeper layers, unstable heads become more functionally important than other heads in the same layer, indicating that instability does not simply identify components with little effect on computation.

Weight decay substantially improves attention-head stability across initializations, while the residual stream is comparatively stable already. These findings distinguish reproducibility of individual heads from stability of the broader representations passing through the network. They motivate testing circuit robustness across independently trained instances before relying on a particular circuit for scalable oversight or conclusions about shared internal mechanisms.
icml-2026-quantifying-llm-attention-head.tldr: Attention heads vary substantially across independent training runs, especially at mid-depth, while weight decay improves stability and residual streams remain comparatively stable.

paragraphs: Language models are used to predict human preferences by generating answers to prompts about people or groups. This paper asks whether internal representations contain useful predictive information that those answers do not fully expose. It introduces mechanistic forecasting and uses election prediction as a test case for examining that possibility.

The study analyzes more than 24 million configurations spanning seven models, six national elections, persona attributes, and prompt variations. It examines how demographic and ideological information activates internal components that encode political parties. Forecasting then draws on that internal knowledge, providing another route from persona information to a preference prediction beyond reading the model’s generated response.

Using internal representations can improve predictive accuracy, but the effect varies across models, countries, parties, and demographic versus opinion-based attributes. The result is therefore a context-dependent empirical gain rather than a universal advantage. It supports the claim that language models contain systematic, usable preference-related information internally and shows why evaluating only their surface outputs can overlook part of their predictive capacity.
icml-2026-reading-between-the-tokens-imp.tldr: Probing language-model representations can improve election preference forecasts, although gains depend on the model, attributes, parties, and national context.

paragraphs: Observational data often identify a family of compatible causal graphs rather than one fully directed graph. Federated causal discovery must also work across clients that keep data decentralized. This paper addresses a complication: different client policies can act as unknown interventions, so assuming every client follows exactly the same causal model can be unrealistic.

The proposed I-PERI algorithm first recovers the partially directed graph common to all clients. It then uses structural differences created by client-level interventions to orient additional edges. Those differences become useful evidence for reducing causal ambiguity. The result is a tighter family of compatible graphs, called the Φ-Markov equivalence class, represented by an augmented partially directed graph called a Φ-CPDAG.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees for I-PERI’s convergence and privacy-preserving properties, together with empirical evaluations showing effectiveness. The intended gain is more informative causal structure under unknown interventions across clients. The output remains an equivalence-class representation, so additional edge orientations narrow the possibilities without implying that every causal direction is necessarily resolved.
icml-2026-regret-based-federated-causal-.tldr: I-PERI uses differences induced by unknown client interventions to refine causal graphs in federated learning, with convergence and privacy guarantees.

paragraphs: High-dimensional observations can lie near a much smaller underlying structure, making geometry useful for understanding their distribution. Standard estimators often build neighbor graphs or kernels, which become expensive as datasets and dimensions grow. This paper proposes learning that geometry with a neural network through a denoising probabilistic framework called Riemannian metric matching.

The network learns the carré du champ operator, a mathematical object that provides access to Riemannian geometry through diffusion geometry. The key step expresses the operator as a conditional expectation over random perturbations of data. That formulation supports training on individual samples and amortized inference at constant cost, without explicitly constructing a kernel for the dataset.

In experiments, metric matching matches or improves the accuracy of k-nearest-neighbor diffusion-geometry estimators while making amortized inference up to 400 times faster. It also supports graph-free analysis of high-dimensional images where nearest-neighbor approaches break down. The result connects a geometric quantity to a learnable prediction task, making repeated access to estimated geometry substantially more efficient in the reported comparisons.
icml-2026-riemannian-metric-matching-for.tldr: Riemannian metric matching learns data geometry without explicit graphs or kernels, with competitive accuracy and up to 400-fold faster amortized inference.

paragraphs: Answering a question from a knowledge graph can require crossing intermediate nodes whose wording barely resembles the question. A retriever that relies too heavily on semantic overlap may miss these bridges. This paper addresses that problem with RSF-GLLM, separating differentiable graph reasoning from the language model that ultimately produces the answer.

Its Recurrent Soft-Flow module propagates continuous relevance scores through the graph. A GRU-guided query updater changes the reasoning state, while dynamic gates use structural cues to traverse semantically dissimilar intermediate nodes. Flow-sparsity regularization provides a theoretical convergence guarantee from soft probabilities to discrete reasoning paths. The extracted paths are converted into text and used to fine-tune the answer-generating model.

This arrangement gives the generator graph-derived reasoning evidence while assigning traversal to a dedicated module. On WebQSP and CWQ, the authors report competitive answer performance and better inference efficiency than computationally expensive LLM-based approaches. The contribution is a way to learn useful graph routes despite lexical gaps and then pass those routes to language generation in an explicit form.
icml-2026-rsf-gllm-bridging-the-semantic.tldr: RSF-GLLM learns graph reasoning paths through semantically dissimilar nodes, then uses those paths to support efficient language-model answer generation.

paragraphs: Diffusion-based imaging reconstruction balances consistency with observed data, classifier-free guidance, and sampling randomness. Their effects depend on when and how strongly each is applied. This paper argues that optimizing the three schedules together is important because treating them separately can miss interactions that shape the entire reconstruction trajectory.

The analysis finds that strong classifier-free guidance early in sampling conflicts with data-consistency guidance, while randomness can move the trajectory back toward higher-probability regions. Triadic Dynamics Aware Posterior Sampling, or TriPS, formulates scheduling as a time-varying control problem. Its schedules follow a trend of decreasing data-consistency and stochasticity scales while increasing the classifier-free guidance scale.

TriPS develops two ways to choose those schedules: searching over functional templates for reliable baseline curves, and using Group Relative Policy Optimization to learn more flexible temporal curves. Experiments report improvements over state-of-the-art baselines in both data fidelity and perceptual realism. The findings emphasize that reconstruction quality depends on coordinating guidance and randomness over time, not just selecting the individual components.
icml-2026-triadic-dynamics-aware-diffusi.tldr: TriPS jointly optimizes data-consistency guidance, classifier-free guidance, and randomness schedules to improve diffusion-based image reconstruction.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning for language-model reasoning often generates the same number of candidate responses for every prompt and learns from sparse success signals. This can waste exploration on some prompts while leaving difficult ones without useful feedback. XRPO reorganizes GRPO around two connected questions: where to spend rollout effort and how to learn more from informative responses.

For exploration, an adaptive allocator prioritizes prompts with greater potential to reduce uncertainty. Curated examples are also supplied in context to help the model make progress on prompts whose rollouts otherwise receive zero reward. For exploitation, a group-relative, novelty-aware mechanism uses sequence likelihoods to strengthen learning from correct responses that the model currently considers unlikely.

Across mathematics and coding benchmarks, covering both reasoning and non-reasoning models, XRPO outperforms methods including GRPO and GSPO. The authors report gains of up to 4% in pass@1 and 6% in cons@32, with convergence accelerated by up to 2.7 times. These are reported maxima across the evaluations, supporting the value of coordinating rollout allocation with richer use of successful responses.
icml-2026-xrpo-pushing-the-limits-of-grp.tldr: XRPO adapts rollout allocation, seeds difficult prompts, and emphasizes unlikely correct responses to improve reasoning performance and training convergence.
